# Renal tubular disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Tubulointerstitial diseases > Renal tubular disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/2l0TwT)

---

## Summary

Renal tubular disorders are a heterogeneous group of diseases that involve dysfunctions of transporters and channels in the renal tubular system. These dysfunctions may cause fluid loss and abnormalities in <u>electrolyte</u> and acid-base <u>homeostasis</u>. The disorders are either primary (genetic) or acquired (e.g., drug adverse effects, renal disease). In <u>renal tubular acidosis</u> (<u>RTA</u>), there is <u>normal anion gap</u> (<u>hyperchloremic</u>) <u>metabolic acidosis</u> in a patient with normal or almost normal renal function. Types of <u>RTA</u> include <u>distal</u> tubular acid secretion (type 1), <u>proximal</u> tubular <u>bicarbonate</u> wasting (type 2), very rarely <u>carbonic anhydrase</u> deficiency (type III), and <u>aldosterone</u> deficiency/resistance (type 4). Type 2 can be further classified into isolated <u>proximal</u> tubular <u>bicarbonate</u> wasting and generalized <u>proximal</u> tubular wasting, known as <u>Fanconi syndrome</u>. X-linked <u>hypophosphatemic</u> <u>rickets</u>, the most common form of <u>hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets</u>, is caused by <u>phosphate</u> wasting and manifests with <u>hypophosphatemia</u> and symptoms of <u>rickets</u>. <u>Bartter syndrome</u>, <u>Liddle syndrome</u>, <u>syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess</u>, and <u>Gitelman syndrome</u> are inherited disorders of tubular function characterized by <u>hypokalemia</u> and <u>metabolic alkalosis</u>. Because renal tubular disorders manifest in heterogeneous ways, diagnosis is often challenging; it is based on a combination of clinical features (e.g., <u>rickets</u>, impaired growth, symptoms of <u>electrolyte</u> deficiencies), <u>laboratory analysis</u> of blood and urine, and the results of investigations aimed at determining an underlying cause. The diagnosis of hereditary conditions is usually confirmed with <u>genetic testing</u>. Treatment of type 1 and <u>type 2 RTA</u> involves alkali therapy, while the treatment of <u>type 4 RTA</u> consists of <u>furosemide</u> therapy. X-linked <u>hypophosphatemic</u> <u>rickets</u> requires the supplementation of <u>phosphate</u> and <u>vitamin D</u>, while the mainstay of therapy for <u>Bartter syndrome</u>, <u>Liddle syndrome</u>, <u>syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess</u>, and <u>Gitelman syndrome</u> involves lifelong oral <u>potassium</u> substitution with <u>potassium-sparing</u> <u>diuretics</u>.

## Renal tubular acidosis (RTA)

* In <u>RTA</u>, there is a <u>normal anion gap metabolic acidosis</u> in patients with normal or almost normal renal function.

* <u>Renal tubular acidosis</u> is caused by defects in the tubular transport of <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> and/or H<sup>+</sup>.

* Most forms of <u>RTA</u> are asymptomatic; rarely, life-threatening <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances may occur.

| Serum <u>potassium</u> levels |  | <br>* <u>Hypokalemia</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hypokalemia</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hypokalemia</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hyperkalemia</u><br><br> |
| <br>Urine <u>pH</u><br> |  | <br>* ≥ 5.5<br><br> | <br><br>* ≥ 5.5: an early finding of <u>proximal RTA</u>; attributed to continuous <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> excretion in the urine<br><br>* < 5.5: typical finding of <u>proximal RTA</u>; attributed to serum <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> depletion<br><br><br> | <br>* ≥ 5.5<br><br> | <br>* < 5.5<br><br> |
| <br><u>Urine anion gap</u> <br> |  | <br>* Positive<br><br> | <br>* Negative<br><br> | <br>* Positive<br><br> | <br>* Positive<br><br> |
| <u>Calcium</u> excretion |  | <br>* Increased<br><br> | <br>* Normal<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> | <br>* Normal or decreased<br><br> |
| Bone involvement |  | <br>* Bone demineralization without overt <u>rickets</u> or <u>osteomalacia</u> (due to increased <u>bone turnover</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Vitamin D</u>-resistant <u>hypophosphatemic</u> <u>rickets</u>/<u>osteomalacia</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Osteopetrosis</u><br><br> | <br>* Bone demineralization without overt <u>rickets</u> or <u>osteomalacia</u><br><br> |
| <u>Nephrolithiasis</u> |  | <br>* Usually present<br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> |

> [!NOTE]
> Patients with uremic <u>acidosis</u> (<u>metabolic acidosis</u> due to <u>renal failure</u>) have a decreased <u>glomerular filtration rate</u> (increased serum <u>creatinine</u>) and <u>increased anion gap metabolic acidosis</u>. Patients with <u>renal tubular acidosis</u> have relatively normal <u>glomerular filtration</u> rates and <u>normal anion gap metabolic acidosis</u>!




> [!NOTE]
> Type 1 <u>RTA</u>: Acid secretion impairment at <u>distal</u> tubule, treatment with Alkali
> Type 2 <u>RTA</u>: Bicarbonate wasting at <u>proximal</u> tubule, treatment with Base (alkali)
> Type 3 <u>RTA</u>: Carbonic anhydrase deficiency, treatment with Citrate (<u>sodium</u>/<u>potassium</u>)
> Type 4 <u>RTA</u>: AlDosterone disorDer, treatment with 4rosemide

## Distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1)

### Pathophysiology




The α-intercalated cells of the <u>distal</u> tubule are unable to secrete H<sup>+</sup> (apical) → ↓ intracellular production of HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>;   → ↓ <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u>/<u>Cl<sup>-</sup></u> exchanger activity (basolateral) → decreased concentration of <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> in the blood → <u>metabolic acidosis</u>




### Etiology




* Sporadic type 1 <u>RTA</u> (<u>idiopathic</u>)

* Familial type 1 <u>RTA</u> (inherited genetic defects)

* Autoimmune diseases

* <u>Systemic lupus erythematosus</u>

* <u>Sjogren syndrome</u>

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>Primary biliary cirrhosis</u>

* <u>Autoimmune hepatitis</u>

* <u>Hashimoto thyroiditis</u>

* <u>Nephrocalcinosis</u> (e.g., <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>, <u>vitamin D</u> toxicity, <u>sarcoidosis</u>)

* <u>Medullary sponge kidney</u>

* Chronic <u>obstructive uropathy</u> (e.g., congenital anomalies)

* <u>Sickle cell</u> nephropathy

* <u>Wilson disease</u>

* Drugs: <u>ifosfamide</u>, <u>amphotericin B</u>; , <u>lithium</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u> (<u>analgesic nephropathy</u>)





### Clinical features




* <u>Nephrocalcinosis</u>: <u>calcium phosphate stones</u>;  (due to an increase in urine <u>pH</u> )

* <u>Polyuria</u> → <u>polydipsia</u>, <u>dehydration</u>

* Bone demineralization;  usually without overt <u>rickets</u> or <u>osteomalacia</u> (due to increased <u>bone turnover</u>)

* Impaired growth

* In some cases, features of <u>hypokalemia</u> (e.g., <u>muscle weakness</u>, <u>hyporeflexia</u>, <u>paralysis</u>, <u>U waves</u> and flattened <u>T waves</u> on <u>ECG</u>)





### Diagnostics




* Serum

* <u>Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis</u> (<u>normal anion gap</u>)

* <u>Hypokalemia</u> that improves with alkaline therapy

* Urine

* Urine <u>pH</u> ≥ 5.5

* Acid load test (<u>ammonium chloride acidification test</u>): Following oral administration of <u>ammonium chloride</u>, the urine does not acidify (<u>pH</u> remains > 5.3).

* Positive <u>urine anion gap</u>

* <u>Hypercalciuria</u>

* Decreased NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> excretion

* Decreased <u>citrate</u> excretion





### Treatment




Alkalinization therapy with orally administered <u>sodium bicarbonate</u> or <u>sodium</u> <u>citrate</u> (Shohl solution)




![Transport in the connecting tubule and collecting duct](media/ay5tk8678bfmrt8baivc1w7q.jpg)

Transport in the connecting tubule and collecting duct




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Renal tubular acidosis</u> type 1 causes <u>kidney</u> stONEs.




References:[[1]](/library/c5aaQO)[[4]](/library/W5aPQO)

## Proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2)

<u>Type 2 renal tubular acidosis</u> is characterized by a dysfunctional <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u> (PCT) that is unable to reabsorb <u>HCO3-</u>. The defect can either be isolated, affecting only the reabsorption of <u>HCO3-</u> or, more commonly, the PCT has a generalized dysfunction of the PCT, in which case the condition is referred to as <u>Fanconi syndrome</u>.




|  | Isolated <u>proximal RTA</u> | <u>Fanconi syndrome</u> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pathophysiology | <br><br>* The <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u> cells are unable to reabsorb <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> leading to increased <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> excretion in the urine.<br><br>* H<sup>+</sup> secretion from α-intercalated cells in the <u>collecting duct</u> can acidify the urine, but cannot compensate for the excessive <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> excretion in the urine, thus resulting in <u>distal</u> tubular <u>acidosis</u>.<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>* Only <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> reabsorption is impaired.<br><br> | <br>* Impaired reabsorption of <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> and other compounds (e.g., <u>potassium</u>, <u>glucose</u>, <u>phosphate</u>, and <u>amino acid</u> reabsorption) in the PCT<br><br> |  |
| <br>Etiology [[3]](/library/d5aoQO) | <br><br>* Sporadic type 2 <u>RTA</u> (<u>idiopathic</u>)<br><br>* Familial type 2 <u>RTA</u> (inherited genetic defects)<br><br>* <u>Autosomal recessive</u> disease (more common)<br><br>* <u>Autosomal dominant</u> disease<br><br>* Drugs: <u>acetazolamide</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Inherited disorders<br><br>* <u>Cystinosis</u><br><br>* Tyrosinemia<br><br>* <u>Galactosemia</u><br><br>* Type 1 <u>glycogen storage disease</u><br><br>* <u>Wilson disease</u><br><br>* <u>Light chain</u> nephropathy (e.g., <u>multiple myeloma</u>)<br><br>* <u>Ischemia</u> (<u>acute tubular necrosis</u>)<br><br>* <u>Amyloidosis</u><br><br>* <u>Vitamin D</u> deficiency<br><br>* <u>Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria</u><br><br>* Drugs: <u>ifosfamide</u>, <u>tenofovir</u>, expired <u>tetracyclines</u>, <u>aminoglycosides</u>, <u>cisplatin</u><br><br>* <u>Heavy metal poisoning</u> (e.g., lead, <u>cadmium</u>, <u>mercury</u>)<br><br><br> |





### Clinical features




* <u>Vitamin D</u>-resistant <u>hypophosphatemic</u> <u>rickets</u>/<u>osteomalacia</u> (caused by phosphaturia and <u>hypophosphatemia</u>; individuals with <u>Fanconi syndrome</u> typically have more severe symptoms)

* <u>Short stature</u>

* <u>Polyuria</u> → <u>polydipsia</u>, <u>dehydration</u>

* In some cases, features of <u>hypokalemia</u> (e.g., <u>muscle weakness</u>, <u>hyporeflexia</u>, <u>paralysis</u>, <u>U waves</u> and flattened <u>T waves</u> on <u>ECG</u>)





### Diagnostics




* Serum

* <u>Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis</u> (i.e., <u>normal anion gap</u>) [[5]](/library/VrXGTz)

* <u>Hypokalemia</u> that worsens with alkali therapy

* <u>Fanconi syndrome</u>

* Hypouricemia

* <u>Hypophosphatemia</u>

* Urine

* Urine <u>pH</u>

* If serum <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> is higher than its reabsorption threshold: <u>pH</u> ≥ 5.5

* If serum <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u> is depleted: <u>pH</u> < 5.5

* <u>Bicarbonate</u> infusion test: Urine <u>pH</u> rises to a level higher than 7.5 and the <u>fractional excretion</u> of <u>bicarbonate</u> is > 15% following administration of <u>IV sodium bicarbonate</u> .

* Negative <u>urine anion gap</u>

* <u>Fanconi syndrome</u>

* <u>Aminoaciduria</u>

* <u>Glucosuria</u> despite normal or low serum <u>glucose</u>

* Phosphaturia





### Treatment




* Alkali therapy with orally administered <u>potassium</u> <u>citrate</u>

* <u>Thiazide diuretics</u> if alkali therapy is not tolerated or effective





![Overview of the proximal convoluted tubule](media/vqodiydlur87m71plgoaezzc.jpg)

Overview of the proximal convoluted tubule




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Renal tubular acidosis</u> type 2 has two variants (isolated <u>proximal RTA</u> and <u>Fanconi syndrome</u>).

## Hyperkalemic renal tubular acidosis (type 4)

### Etiology




* <u>Hypoaldosteronism</u>

* <u>Primary adrenal insufficiency</u> (<u>Addison disease</u>)

* <u>Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism</u>

* Acute <u>glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>Diabetic nephropathy</u> (diabetic hyporeninism)

* <u>SLE</u>

* <u>AIDS</u> nephropathy

* Drugs: <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>cyclosporin</u>

* Drugs: <u>ARBs</u>, <u>ACE inhibitors</u>, <u>heparin</u>  [[6]](/library/drXoTz)

* Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 (<u>Gordon syndrome</u>)

* An <u>autosomal dominant</u> condition characterized by increased <u>sodium</u> reabsorption and decreased <u>potassium</u> secretion due to dysfunction of ion channels in the <u>kidney</u>.

* Manifestations include <u>hypertension</u>, <u>hyperkalemia</u>, <u>hyperchloremia</u>, and <u>metabolic acidosis</u>.

* <u>Aldosterone</u> resistance

* Chronic <u>obstructive nephropathy</u> or <u>interstitial</u> nephropathy

* Drugs: <u>Potassium-sparing</u> <u>diuretics</u> (e.g., <u>spironolactone</u>, <u>amiloride</u>, <u>eplerenone</u>, <u>triamterene</u>), <u>trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole</u>, <u>pentamidine</u>

* Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1: A form of <u>aldosterone</u> resistance that is a caused by an <u>autosomal dominant</u> <u>loss-of-function</u> mutation in the <u>gene</u> encoding for <u>mineralocorticoid</u> <u>receptor</u> protein or <u>autosomal recessive</u> <u>loss-of-function</u> mutations in the <u>genes</u> encoding the <u>epithelial sodium channel</u>.





### Pathophysiology




<u>Aldosterone</u> deficiency and/or resistance in the <u>collecting duct</u> and <u>distal convoluted tubules</u>;   → <u>hyperkalemia</u>;  and metabolic <u>acidosis</u> → inhibition of <u>ammonia</u> (<u>NH<sub>3</sub></u>) synthesis in the <u>proximal convoluted tubules</u>;   → decreased urinary ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) excretion




### Clinical features




* <u>Renal insufficiency</u>: <u>polyuria</u> → <u>polydipsia</u>, <u>dehydration</u>

* Impaired <u>growth in children</u>

* Features of <u>hyperkalemia</u> (e.g., <u>muscle weakness</u>, prolonged <u>PR interval</u> and peaked <u>T waves</u> on <u>ECG</u>)





### Diagnostics




* Serum

* <u>Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis</u>;  (i.e., <u>normal anion gap</u>)

* <u>Hyperkalemia</u>

* Urine

* Urine <u>pH</u> < 5.5

* Positive <u>urine anion gap</u> (persistent <u>sodium</u> excretion)

* Decreased NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> excretion

* Normal or decreased <u>calcium</u> excretion





### Treatment




* <u>Furosemide</u>

* <u>Mineralocorticoid</u> replacement (<u>fludrocortisone</u>)

* Low-<u>potassium</u> diet





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Renal tubular acidosis</u> type 4 leads to decreased NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> excretion.

---

## X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets

### Etiology




X-linked dominant disease caused by a mutation in the PHEX <u>gene</u>




### Pathophysiology




Mutation in the PHEX <u>gene</u> → increased levels of <u>fibroblast growth factor 23</u> (<u>FGF23</u>)  → indirect inhibition of the <u>sodium</u>-<u>phosphate</u> cotransporter in the <u>proximal</u> renal tubule → impaired reabsorption of <u>phosphate</u> → chronic <u>hypophosphatemia</u> → <u>vitamin D</u>-resistant <u>rickets</u>/<u>osteomalacia</u>




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* X-linked <u>hypophosphatemic</u> <u>rickets</u> accounts for ∼ 80% of all familial <u>causes of hypophosphatemia</u>.

* Age of symptom onset: typically < 3 years





### Clinical features




* Features of <u>rickets</u> (e.g., <u>short stature</u>, bowing of legs)

* Dental <u>abscesses</u>

* Calcification of <u>soft tissues</u> (<u>tendons</u>, <u>ligaments</u>, and <u>joint capsules</u>)

* <u>Deafness</u>

* <u>Arnold-Chiari</u> <u>malformation</u>





### Diagnostics




* Laboratory tests

* Pronounced <u>hypophosphatemia</u>

* Increased <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>

* Decreased or normal <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u>

* Normal serum <u>calcium</u>, <u>parathyroid hormone</u>/parathyroid <u>hormone</u>-related <u>peptide</u>, and 25-dihydroxyvitamin D

* <u>X-ray</u> of the wrists, knees, ankles, and <u>long bones</u>, such as the <u>femur</u> (See “Diagnostics” in <u>osteomalacia and rickets</u>.)





### Treatment




* Burosumab

* Drug of choice for children aged ≥ 1 year

* A <u>monoclonal antibody</u> that targets <u>FGF23</u>

* <u>Phosphate</u> substitution

* <u>Calcitriol</u> (<u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u>) substitution

* Complications of treatment: <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>, <u>nephrocalcinosis</u>
* <u>Amiloride</u> and <u>hydrochlorothiazide</u> are used to increase <u>calcium</u> reabsorption and thereby lower the risk of <u>nephrocalcinosis</u>.





![Affected regions of a nephron in renal tubular defects](media/kfl860kitzaxofooymme86cl.jpg)

Affected regions of a nephron in renal tubular defects

## Bartter syndrome

### Definition




A group of rare genetic disorders (<u>autosomal recessive</u>);  that affect <u>chloride</u> reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the <u>loop of Henle</u>




### <u>Epidemiology</u>



* <u>Prevalence</u>: 1/1,000,000




### Pathophysiology




Defective <u>Na<sup>+</sup>-K<sup>+</sup>-2Cl<sup>-</sup> cotransporter</u> in the thick <u>ascending loop of Henle</u>   results in:




* Loss of <u>Cl<sup>-</sup></u>, Na<sup>+</sup>, and <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> in urine (as seen in chronic <u>loop diuretic</u> use)

* Failure to reabsorb Na<sup>+</sup> leading to <u>natriuresis</u> (salt and water loss) and <u>volume depletion</u>, which activates the <u>renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system</u> (<u>RAAS</u>), leading to

* Renal <u>vasoconstriction</u>; however, a rise in <u>prostaglandin</u> E levels to counter renal <u>vasoconstriction</u> results in growth inhibition

* Elevated <u>aldosterone</u> levels, leading to increased <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> and H<sup>+</sup> excretion and subsequent <u>hypokalemia</u> and <u>metabolic alkalosis</u>

* Decreased paracellular reabsorption of <u>calcium</u>;   → <u>hypercalciuria</u> → <u>hypocalcemia</u>, <u>nephrocalcinosis</u>, and <u>renal stones</u>





### Clinical features




* Antenatal symptoms: <u>polyhydramnios</u>, <u>preterm delivery</u>

* Severe <u>polyuria</u>;  and <u>polydipsia</u>;  → life-threatening <u>volume depletion</u> and <u>hypotension</u>

* Muscle <u>atrophy</u>, <u>weakness</u>, cramps, <u>carpopedal spasm</u>

* <u>Failure to thrive</u>, <u>developmental delay</u>

* Dysmorphic facies  , <u>strabismus</u>, <u>sensorineural deafness</u>

* Symptoms of <u>renal colic</u> may occur as a result of <u>calcium</u> stones.





### Diagnostics




* Laboratory diagnostics

* <u>Metabolic alkalosis</u>

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* <u>Hypercalciuria</u>

* <u>Hyperuricemia</u> (∼ 50% of cases)

* Response to <u>thiazide</u> and <u>loop diuretics</u> 

* Normal response to <u>thiazide diuretics</u>

* Blunted response to <u>loop diuretics</u>

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>genetic testing</u>





### Treatment



* Mainstay of therapy: : lifelong oral <u>potassium</u> substitution with <u>potassium-sparing</u> <u>diuretics</u> (<u>spironolactone</u>, <u>amiloride</u>)




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>Na-K-2Cl cotransporter</u> that is defective in <u>Bartter syndrome</u> is a target for <u>loop diuretics</u>!




References:[[9]](/library/25aTjO)[[10]](/library/f5akjO)

---

## Gitelman syndrome

### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>Prevalence</u>: 1/40,000

* Age of symptom onset: ≥ 6 years; diagnosis is usually made in <u>adolescence</u> or adulthood





### Etiology




<u>Autosomal recessive</u>;  defect in the <u>SLC12A3</u> <u>gene</u> on <u>chromosome</u> 16p → impaired function of the <u>thiazide</u>-sensitive <u>sodium-chloride cotransporter</u> in the <u>distal convoluted tubule</u> → impaired Na<sup>+</sup> and <u>Cl<sup>-</sup></u> reabsorption → mild <u>natriuresis</u> → mild volume depletion → mild <u>RAAS</u> activation




### Clinical features



* Clinical features are similar to those of chronic <u>thiazide diuretic</u> use:

* Fatigue, <u>muscle weakness</u>

* Muscle cramps and/or <u>tetany</u>

* Mild <u>polyuria</u>

* <u>Chondrocalcinosis</u>

* In some cases, mild <u>hypotension</u>




### Diagnostics




* <u>Metabolic alkalosis</u>

* Severe <u>hypokalemia</u>

* <u>Hypercalcemia</u> and hypocalciuria

* <u>Hypomagnesemia</u>

* Response to <u>thiazide</u> and <u>loop diuretics</u> 

* Normal response to <u>loop diuretics</u>

* Blunted response to <u>thiazide diuretics</u>

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>genetic testing</u>





### Treatment



* Mainstay of therapy: : lifelong oral <u>potassium</u> substitution with <u>potassium-sparing diuretics</u> (<u>spironolactone</u>, <u>amiloride</u>)




> [!NOTE]
> The effects of <u>Gitelman syndrome</u> are similar to those of a <u>thiazide diuretic</u>!




References:[[10]](/library/f5akjO)

---

## Liddle syndrome

### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Extremely rare

* Age of symptom onset: childhood





### Etiology




<u>Autosomal dominant</u> <u>gain-of-function</u> mutation;  in the SCNN1B and SCNN1G <u>genes</u> on <u>chromosome</u> 16p → structural alteration in the β and γ subunits of the <u>epithelial sodium channel</u> (<u>ENaC</u>) in the <u>collecting duct</u>




### Pathophysiology




Structural alteration in the <u>ENaC</u> subunits → inability of these subunits to bind with an intracellular <u>ubiquitin</u>-protein ligase (Nedd4) → decreased degradation of <u>ENaC channels</u> by <u>ubiquitin</u> <u>proteasomes</u>;  → increased number of <u>ENaCs</u> in the collecting duct → increased reuptake of water and <u>sodium</u> (<u>pseudohyperaldosteronism</u>) → <u>hypertension</u> with low <u>renin</u> production and <u>hypokalemia</u>




### Clinical features



* <u>Hypertension</u>




### Diagnostics




* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* <u>Metabolic alkalosis</u>

* Decreased <u>renin</u> and <u>aldosterone</u> levels

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>genetic testing</u>





### Treatment




Lifelong oral <u>potassium</u> substitution with <u>potassium-sparing diuretics</u> that directly block <u>ENaCs</u> in the <u>collecting duct</u> (e.g., <u>amiloride</u>, <u>triamterene</u>)




> [!NOTE]
> The clinical features of <u>Liddle syndrome</u> are similar to those of hyperaldosteronism, except that <u>Liddle syndrome</u> manifests with decreased <u>renin</u> and <u>aldosterone</u> levels!

## Syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess

### <u>Epidemiology</u> (hereditary disorder) [[11]](/library/5IYiWq)




* Extremely rare

* Age of symptom onset: <u>infancy</u>





### Etiology




* <u>Autosomal recessive</u>; , <u>loss-of-function</u> mutations in the <u>11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase</u> type 2 (11-beta-HSD2) <u>gene</u> on <u>chromosome</u> 16q → ↓ 11-beta-HSD2 enzyme.

* Acquired disorder from chronic exposure to glycyrrhetinic acid (e.g., from excessive consumption of black licorice), which inhibits the activity of the 11-beta-HSD2 enzyme.





### Pathophysiology




* With normal 11-beta-HSD2 activity: 11-beta-HSD2 converts <u>cortisol</u> into <u>cortisone</u> (<u>cortisone</u>, unlike <u>cortisol</u>, does not activate <u>mineralocorticoid</u> <u>receptors</u>).

* With <u>11-beta-HSD2 deficiency</u> (or inhibition): ↓ <u>cortisol</u> conversion to <u>cortisone</u> → ↑ <u>cortisol</u> → ↑ <u>mineralocorticoid</u> <u>receptor</u> activity.





### Clinical features




* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* <u>Failure to thrive</u>

* <u>Muscle weakness</u>

* <u>Polyuria</u> and <u>polydipsia</u> due to <u>nephrogenic diabetes insipidus</u>

* <u>Renal failure</u>





### Diagnostics




* Best initial test: high <u>ratio</u> of urinary free <u>cortisol</u> to <u>cortisone</u> in a 24-hour urine collection

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>genetic testing</u>

* Additional findings

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* <u>Metabolic alkalosis</u>

* Decreased <u>renin</u> and <u>aldosterone</u> levels

* Decreased urinary free <u>cortisone</u> excretion

* <u>Hypercalciuria</u>





### Treatment




* Cessation of licorice ingestion

* Lifelong oral <u>potassium</u> substitution with <u>potassium-sparing</u> <u>diuretics</u> (e.g., <u>amiloride</u> or <u>eplerenone</u>) to decrease the <u>mineralocorticoid</u> effects

* <u>Thiazide</u> in <u>hypercalciuria</u> or <u>nephrocalcinosis</u>

* <u>Corticosteroids</u>; : <u>Exogenous</u> <u>corticosteroid</u> decreases <u>endogenous</u> <u>cortisol</u> production and subsequently reduces <u>mineralocorticoid</u> <u>receptor</u> activation.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Spironolactone</u> (an <u>aldosterone receptor antagonist</u>) is effective in treating the <u>syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess</u> but not <u>Liddle syndrome</u>!




> [!NOTE]
> In Syndrome of Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess, <u>cortisol</u> has the SAME action as <u>aldosterone</u>.
